title: RAW UNREVIEWED: Vitruvius vermilion: exposure changes wall colour unless a later coating protects it
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED_NOT_SELECTED_NOT_TESTED. The same vermilion finish retains colour indoors but blackens in exposed settings; a coating applied after the wall is dry is intended to preserve its colour. Separate preventive overcoating from repainting an already damaged wall with other colours.

source.span: VII.9.1–4, preparation, indoor/outdoor contrast, Faberius example and ganosis
source.layer: Historical primary work in an explicitly named translation; source content inspected, no medieval Voynich ownership implied

differentiating_relation: PIGMENT coats WALL; EXPOSURE changes that finish, while WAX_OIL_COAT applied after drying is assigned a protective role. A reported failed exposed wall and its later repainting are a separate episode, not evidence that wax reverses blackening.
complete_source_account: VII.9.1 binds repeated washing/heating to pigment preparation and describes the loss of quicksilver.
VII.9.2 contrasts closed and open settings and reports Faberius replacing a mottled finish after thirty days.
VII.9.3–4 prescribe the dry-wall overcoat, warming and rubbing sequence and state its protective purpose.
known_counterexplanation: A pigment-name substitution account calls the black and red states different materials. A repair account has wax turn an already black wall red again. A universal-light rule predicts indoor and coated walls behave like the unprotected exposed finish.
